doc.title: David Spinozza interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, NY, September 27, 2025

title: Learning to write for horns from guitar voicings
summary: He took theory in high school and wrote for four or five horns at 13-14, using guitar voicings; for two horns he uses the third and seventh.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So where did you access in your head how to write for horns? Was there something you heard growing up that you were paying attention to?

Well I always listened – I used to listen to – it was funny, even some of my guitar lines come from horn players. I got most of how I play jazz from listening to horn players. Like I would listen to Lee Morgan for instance like that, I had that record “Sidewinder” you know. And I’d arranged that a few times for my band. But I was studying music theory in high school. I had a really good music theory teacher. So he would teach me how to take dictation, how to write stuff out, and so I was learning how to do that anyway, and I sort of led off the guitar, like the voicings on the guitar are almost like drop two voicings which, you know, is a big band style of writing. And I would just write stuff off the guitar and write it out for horn players and they’d play it and it sounded good. And I was able to make four horns sound pretty big just because of the voicings. So I started that at like 13, 14 years old I was already writing for horns and stuff with my band. So I’ve always had like two trumpets, an alto sax, a bari and a tenor or something, you know four or five horns. And that’s how I started writing.
If you’re writing for just two, did you discover like what’s the most effective thing of the notes in the chord – if it’s just two horns.

Two horns to me, it’s always the third and the seventh. You know the first thing I would do is drop the tonic, you know, drop the fifth, you don’t need that. It’s going to be implied in the piano part and the bass line and this and that. So it was always like yeah, the third and the seventh.
